questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes governance from management?
options: Governance is performed by the security team; management is performed by the board
Governance concerns technical controls; management concerns business processes
Governance sets direction, assigns accountability and provides oversight; management executes within that direction
Governance applies to regulated organisations only; management applies to all organisations
questions.explanation: The board governs — it decides the risk appetite, approves policy and holds management to account. Management executes. (A) inverts the roles, which is the most commonly chosen wrong answer because the security team is more visible than the board.

questions.stem: An organisation passes every requirement of its regulatory audit and is breached six weeks later through a weakness the audit did not examine. Which principle does this best illustrate?
options: Compliance is a minimum baseline assessed at a point in time, and is not the same as security
The audit was performed negligently and the auditor bears responsibility
Regulatory frameworks are unsuitable for measuring security posture
The organisation's risk appetite was set too high
questions.explanation: Compliance demonstrates that a defined set of requirements was met on a given day; attackers are not limited to that set. (C) overreaches — frameworks are useful, they are simply not exhaustive. Nothing in the scenario supports (B) or (D).

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument for running governance, risk and compliance as one integrated programme rather than three separate functions?
options: It reduces the number of staff required in the security team
It removes the need for external audit
It guarantees regulatory penalties will not be imposed
A single control can be mapped once and tested once while satisfying several obligations, reducing duplicated effort and giving one consistent view of risk
questions.explanation: "Map once, test once, report many" is the core efficiency argument, and the single view of risk is the effectiveness argument. (A) is a possible side effect but not the purpose; (B) and (C) claim outcomes GRC cannot deliver — note the absolute language in (C).

questions.stem: Who is responsible for setting an organisation's risk appetite?
options: The information security manager, as the subject-matter expert
Senior leadership and the board, as part of the governance function
The internal audit function, based on prior findings
Each individual risk owner, for the risks they own
questions.explanation: Appetite is a strategic statement about how much risk the organisation will pursue in pursuit of its objectives — only leadership can make it. (D) is the near-miss: risk owners operate within the appetite and accept individual residual risks, but they do not define the appetite itself.

questions.stem: Which framework is specifically concerned with the governance and management of enterprise IT and its alignment to business objectives?
options: COBIT
ISO/IEC 27002
NIST SP 800-88
OWASP Top 10
questions.explanation: COBIT — (B) is a code of practice for security controls, not IT governance. (C) covers media sanitisation and (D) web application risks — both are real documents placed here because recognising what a framework is for is the actual skill being tested.

questions.stem: An organisation begins using a third-party generative AI service. Under the 2026 outline, how should it be treated within the GRC programme?
options: As an exception, since AI services cannot be assessed with conventional risk methods
As out of scope until a dedicated AI governance framework is adopted
As an asset like any other — recorded in the inventory, subject to existing policy and legal obligations, and tracked through the risk register
As a purely technical matter for the engineering team, outside the governance remit
questions.explanation: The outline's position is explicitly that AI tools "are subject to the same organizational policies and legal requirements as traditional software". (B) is the seductive answer because a dedicated framework is good practice — but waiting for one means the risk goes ungoverned in the meantime.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a risk register?
options: To record every security incident that has occurred, with its root cause
To provide a single living record of identified risks, their owners, treatments, status and residual level
To list the controls in place so that auditors can sample them
To document the organisation's risk appetite and tolerance statements
questions.explanation: Ownership and status are what make it a management tool rather than a list. (A) describes an incident log, (C) a control register or SoA, and (D) the risk appetite statement — three real artefacts that each do something a register does not.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: Which activity produces the recovery objectives used by continuity and recovery plans?
options: The risk assessment
The disaster recovery test
The threat model
The business impact analysis
questions.explanation: The BIA — It identifies critical functions and the impact of losing them over time, from which RTO, RPO and MTD are derived. (A) is the strongest distractor — a risk assessment is closely related and often runs alongside, but it measures risk, not tolerable downtime and data loss.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: A payments platform states that in a disaster it can afford to lose no more than five minutes of transaction data. Which objective does this define, and what does it drive?
options: RPO — it drives how frequently data must be backed up or replicated
RTO — it drives how quickly the service must be restored
MTD — it drives the maximum permissible outage before the business fails
MTTR — it drives the average time engineers take to complete a repair
questions.explanation: RPO — Point = the point in the past you can afford to roll back to, so it governs backup or replication frequency. Five minutes of tolerable data loss effectively mandates continuous replication rather than nightly backups. Swapping RPO and RTO is the most common error in this domain.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: How do RTO and MTD relate to one another?
options: They are the same figure expressed from different perspectives
RTO must be shorter than MTD, so that recovery completes before the business suffers critical harm
MTD must be shorter than RTO, since it represents the hard limit on the recovery team
They are independent, since RTO concerns technology and MTD concerns data
questions.explanation: MTD is the point of unacceptable harm; RTO is the target you set to stay inside it, with margin. (C) is the inversion. (D) misstates both — MTD is a business measure and RTO a recovery target; neither is about data, which is RPO.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: A recovery facility has power, cooling, network connectivity and floor space, but no installed servers or data. What is it, and what is its main trade-off?
options: A hot site — fastest to activate, highest cost
A warm site — moderate cost, hours to days to activate
A cold site — cheapest to maintain, but days to weeks before it can carry production
A mirrored site — continuous replication with no data loss
questions.explanation: Cold site — The presence of facilities but absence of equipment and data is the definition. (B) is the near-miss and worth pinning down: a warm site has hardware and connectivity installed but needs data restored.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: Which backup strategy produces the fastest nightly backup but the slowest restore?
options: Full backups every night
Differential backups against a weekly full
Continuous data protection with journaling
Incremental backups against a weekly full
questions.explanation: Incremental — Each job copies only what changed since the last backup of any type, so nightly jobs are small — but a restore needs the last full plus every subsequent incremental in sequence. (B) is the mirror image: differentials grow larger each night but restore from just the full plus the latest differential.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: Which statement about business continuity and disaster recovery is correct?
options: They are independent programmes addressing different categories of event
DR is a subset of BC — BC keeps the business operating, DR restores the technology
BC is a subset of DR — DR is the broader organisational programme
BC addresses natural disasters; DR addresses cyber incidents
questions.explanation: BC is the wider programme covering people, premises, processes and suppliers; DR is the technology-recovery component within it. (C) is the inversion, and (D) invents a split by event type that does not exist — both plans apply regardless of cause.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: An organisation keeps three copies of its data on two media types with one copy offsite, and is still encrypted end-to-end by ransomware including its backups. Which additional practice would most likely have prevented this?
options: Keeping at least one copy offline or immutable, so it cannot be reached or altered by the attacker
Increasing the number of copies from three to five
Shortening the RPO so that backups run more frequently
Moving all backup copies to a single cloud provider for consistency
questions.explanation: Modern ransomware deliberately seeks out and encrypts reachable backups, which is why the 3-2-1 rule is now commonly written 3-2-1-1-0 — one copy offline or immutable, zero errors on restore testing. (C) makes the problem worse by producing more encrypted copies faster.

questions.topic: Redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery
questions.stem: What is the difference between high availability and fault tolerance?
options: High availability applies to hardware; fault tolerance applies to software
They are synonyms, with fault tolerance being the older term
High availability minimises downtime through rapid failover; fault tolerance allows the system to continue with no interruption at all
High availability protects against natural failure; fault tolerance protects against deliberate attack
questions.explanation: The distinction is whether the user perceives an interruption. HA accepts a brief failover window; fault tolerance is engineered so the failure is invisible — at considerably greater cost. (D) invents a cause-based split that does not exist.

questions.stem: Which correctly orders awareness, training and education by depth and purpose?
options: Training changes what people notice; awareness builds specific skills; education is refresher content
All three are synonyms for mandatory annual security content
Education is delivered first to build context, then training, then awareness reinforcement
Awareness changes what people notice; training builds role-specific skills; education develops underlying understanding
questions.explanation: Awareness is broad and continuous for everyone; training is role-based and skills-focused; education is deeper conceptual learning for practitioners. (A) is the swap of the first two, which is the trap. (C) inverts the sequence — you do not start an entire workforce with formal education.

questions.stem: After an employee reports that they clicked a phishing link, they are formally disciplined. What is the most likely consequence for the organisation's security posture?
options: Improved posture, as the deterrent effect will reduce future click rates
Weakened posture, because staff will stop reporting and incidents will be discovered later
No material change, since technical controls determine posture
Improved posture, provided the discipline is applied consistently
questions.explanation: Punishing the reporter optimises for silence, not safety. Time-to-report is one of the most valuable metrics a security programme has, and a blame-free reporting culture is what protects it. (A) and (D) confuse deterring the click with deterring the report — only the latter is actually being punished here.

questions.stem: An accounts payable clerk receives an email that appears to be from the CFO, referencing a real acquisition currently under way, asking for an urgent transfer to a new supplier account before close of business. Which term best describes this?
options: Business email compromise, using pretexting and appeals to authority and urgency
Vishing, since the request concerns a financial transaction
Baiting, since the attacker offers something the target wants
Shoulder surfing, since the attacker knew details of the acquisition
questions.explanation: BEC is the specific term for impersonating an executive or supplier to trigger a fraudulent payment, and the levers are authority (the CFO) and urgency (before close of business). (D) is included because candidates reach for it to explain how the attacker knew the detail — but the knowledge more likely came from open-source research, and shoulder surfing describes direct observation.

questions.stem: An employee holds a secure door open for a colleague they recognise but who has forgotten their badge. What is this, and what is the correct response?
options: Tailgating — and it is acceptable where the person is personally known
Shoulder surfing — the colleague should re-badge at the next reader
Piggybacking — the entry was consented to, and it defeats access logging regardless of who the person is
Impersonation — the colleague has assumed another identity to gain entry
questions.explanation: Consent makes it piggybacking rather than tailgating; the security failure is identical, because the access log now shows one person entering where two did. (A)'s second clause is the trap — familiarity is exactly the lever social engineers exploit, and an access control vestibule exists to remove the judgement call entirely.

questions.stem: Why does the 2026 outline specifically call out AI in the context of security awareness?
options: Because AI-generated phishing is easier to detect through automated filtering
Because awareness training can now be fully automated and delivered by AI
Because AI systems, not people, are now the primary target of social engineering
Because generative AI makes phishing and pretexting fluent, personalised and scalable, and enables deepfake voice and video impersonation
questions.explanation: The traditional tells — poor grammar, generic greetings, awkward phrasing — no longer reliably identify a phishing email, so training must shift toward verifying requests through a known second channel. (A) states the opposite of the problem.

questions.stem: Staff repeatedly enter credentials into convincing phishing pages despite email filtering, endpoint protection and a web proxy being in place. Which control most directly addresses the remaining weakness?
options: Deploying an additional layer of email filtering from a second vendor
A sustained security awareness programme with simulations, coaching and easy reporting — supported by phishing-resistant MFA
Blocking all inbound email containing hyperlinks
Increasing the frequency of vulnerability scanning across the estate
questions.explanation: The vulnerability described is human, so the primary control must be administrative — with a technical backstop that removes the value of a stolen password. (C) is the over-correction that fails a business feasibility test; (D) addresses an entirely different weakness.

questions.stem: "Number of internet-facing systems running end-of-life software, with escalation to the risk committee above ten" is best classified as:
options: A key performance indicator
A compliance metric
A key risk indicator
A service level objective
questions.explanation: KRI — Two signals give it away: it is forward-looking — it describes exposure that has not yet caused harm — and it has a defined threshold that triggers escalation. (A) would measure how well a process performed, looking backwards.

questions.stem: "Percentage of critical patches deployed within the 14-day SLA during the last quarter" is best classified as:
options: A key performance indicator
A key risk indicator
A risk appetite statement
A control objective
questions.explanation: KPI — It looks backwards at how well a process performed against a target. The same underlying subject can yield both: unpatched critical vulnerabilities currently open would be the corresponding KRI, since it describes present exposure rather than past performance.

questions.stem: A board asks for regular visibility of the security programme. Which reporting vehicle best suits that audience, and why?
options: An operational dashboard, because near-real-time data is the most accurate
A raw export of SIEM alert counts, because it is unfiltered and objective
A weekly incident ticket queue, because it shows current workload
A periodic scorecard expressing risk in business terms against strategic objectives, with trend direction
questions.explanation: Boards need direction of travel and business consequence, not volumes. (A) is the strongest distractor — dashboards are genuinely valuable, but for operational and management audiences who can act on minute-by-minute data. Matching vehicle to audience is the skill being tested.

questions.stem: Which quality most distinguishes a useful security metric from a merely accurate one?
options: That it is expressed as a percentage rather than an absolute count
That it is actionable — someone can change a decision or behaviour in response to it
That it is collected automatically without manual effort
That it can be benchmarked against industry peers
questions.explanation: A number nobody can act on is decoration, however precise. (C) and (D) are genuine desirable properties, which is what makes them good distractors — but automation and benchmarking improve a metric that is already actionable rather than substituting for it.
